turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I dare say, you are quite familiar with Mr. Wickham's misfortunes, having been a close acquaintance of his and having, no doubt, encouraged his behavior.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I fail to see how my acquaintance with Mr. Wickham, or my attempts to prevent his scandalous behavior, can be held against me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You would have me believe that your interference was motivated by a desire to do good, rather than to protect your own family's reputation?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find it distressing that you should question my motivations, especially after I have taken the liberty of declaring my love for you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I find it quite astonishing that you would think me so foolish as to be swayed by your declarations of love, after all that has passed between us.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you consider the reasons behind my actions, rather than making assumptions based on your own prejudices and misconceptions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not 'consider' your actions, Mr. Darcy, because I have seen through the facade of your pride and prejudices. Your interference in Wickham's affairs was indeed motivated by a desire to protect your own family's reputation, and I will not be swayed by your feeble attempts to rewrite history.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your obstinacy, Miss Elizabeth, is quite remarkable, and I fear it shall prove to be a barrier to our understanding, as well as to any potential union between us.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Darcy, that I am more concerned with the sincerity of your feelings than with your ability to understand me, for it is clear that you have yet to grasp the depth of my own feelings on the matter.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I find it increasingly difficult to comprehend the vehemence of your objections, particularly given that I have endeavored to make amends for past transgressions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no interest in amends, Mr. Darcy, nor in a union with someone who has so callously disregarded the feelings of others for the sake of his own pride.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your sentiments, Miss Elizabeth, are as predictable as they are misguided. I must admit that I find it peculiar that you should continue to cling to your misapprehensions of my character.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Darcy, that your notion of amends is a farce, and it is precisely this lack of genuine remorse that convinces me of your true character.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your obstinacy, Miss Elizabeth, is quite remarkable, and I daresay, it will not serve you well to persist in your refusal of my hand.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must insist that you do not attempt to lecture me on my character, Mr. Darcy, when your own behavior has been so flagrantly self-serving.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: It is not for you, Miss Elizabeth, to dictate what is or is not suitable for me, when it comes to matters of my own heart and intentions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no interest in the whims of your heart, Mr. Darcy, and I certainly do not consider myself bound by your notions of propriety or social standing.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that your continued refusal to consider my proposal only serves to confirm my initial impression of you: that you are a woman of limited understanding and sensibility, utterly unprepared to navigate the complexities of life at Pemberley.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How dare you, Mr. Darcy, suggest that I am unprepared for life at Pemberley, when it is you who have consistently demonstrated a lack of empathy and understanding for the lives and feelings of others?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Miss Elizabeth, that your vitriolic tongue only serves to underscore the gravity of my decision to propose to you, despite the evident difficulties and challenges that your character presents.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
